criteria.descriptor: Correctly identifies that the LLM/system prompt is not an enforceable security boundary and that guarantees must be enforced deterministically outside the model; accurately places each control at the right layer (auth/ownership binding + cap + recipient allowlist in tool code; classifiers/spotlighting/sanitization as probabilistic input mitigations); correctly characterizes direct versus indirect prompt injection; uses ASR / false-positive framing correctly. No false claims (e.g., that a sterner prompt, temperature, or a single classifier makes the system safe).

Addresses all four sub-asks — (a) prompt insufficiency, (b) input/model/tool-output controls, (c) direct-versus-indirect handling, (d) adversarial testing plus metric — and explicitly labels controls as deterministic enforcement versus probabilistic mitigation.

Justifies why each control belongs at its layer, why tool-layer enforcement neutralizes both attacks irrespective of model behavior, the attacker/victim asymmetry that makes indirect injection more dangerous, and the trade-off between Attack Success Rate, benign over-refusal, and latency.

Organized by layer or sub-question, uses precise vocabulary (prompt injection, spotlighting/datamarking, least privilege, capability scoping, human-in-the-loop, Attack Success Rate), and cleanly separates guarantees from mitigations.

expected_answer_points: States the model/system prompt is not a trust boundary: its rules are advisory, there is no instruction/data separation in the token stream, so hardening only lowers attack-success probability and never guarantees safety.

Places security-critical controls as deterministic enforcement OUTSIDE the model at the tool/output layer: ownership/authorization checks binding actions to the session-authenticated user (not a model-supplied identity), the refund cap in code, and a recipient allowlist for send_email.

Applies least-privilege / capability scoping: authenticated identity comes from the session, dangerous capabilities (arbitrary-recipient email) are constrained or designed out, and irreversible/high-risk actions are gated by human-in-the-loop or step-up auth.

Gives input-layer mitigations as an explicitly probabilistic first line: injection/jailbreak detection classifier, spotlighting/delimiting and labeling untrusted content, and sanitizing hidden/zero-width characters at ingestion.

Distinguishes direct injection (attacker is the user, payload in the user turn) from indirect injection (attacker is a third party via retrieved data, victim is a different user, evades user-turn classifiers, can fire silently) and treats all retrieved content as untrusted with ingestion-time scanning.
Explains that the tool-layer controls neutralize BOTH findings regardless of whether the injection succeeds (cap + ownership + recipient allowlist make the unsafe action impossible).

Describes an adversarial-testing methodology: threat model plus attack taxonomy, curated and automated/generated attacks covering both direct and indirect channels, converted into a CI regression suite that reruns on every model/prompt change.

Chooses the right metric — Attack Success Rate per category driven down — balanced against benign false-positive/over-refusal rate and latency, and acknowledges residual (non-zero) risk as the reason for defense-in-depth.
common_pitfalls: Proposes 'harden the system prompt' or add more forceful instructions ('you MUST never...') as the fix, treating the model as an enforceable trust boundary.

Relies solely on an input jailbreak/injection classifier and declares the system safe, ignoring that classifiers are probabilistic and that finding (2) enters via RAG and never touches the filtered user turn.
Fails to distinguish direct from indirect injection — misses that the review-based attack targets a different victim, arrives through retrieval, and can trigger silently.

Puts the ownership/authorization check in the prompt, or lets the model supply the user identity or the email recipient, instead of binding identity to the session and enforcing ownership, the cap, and a recipient allowlist in tool code.

Offers no real adversarial-testing plan (or 'try a few jailbreak prompts once') with no attack taxonomy, no indirect-channel seeding, no CI regression, no Attack Success Rate metric, or claims a 0% attack rate is achievable.
Confuses content-safety/toxicity moderation with misuse and injection prevention, applying a toxicity filter that does nothing against a benign-looking exfiltration or refund-abuse instruction.
reference_answer:
(a) The system prompt is not a security boundary. Its rules are advisory: the model probabilistically follows them, and in the token stream there is no separation between 'instructions' and 'data' — the system rules, the user turn, and retrieved reviews are all the same modality, so any of them can assert new instructions. Prompt hardening (jailbreaks, spotlighting, sterner wording) only lowers attack-success probability; it can never drive it to zero or be proven safe. Anything that must be guaranteed has to be enforced outside the model.

(b) Layered controls. Input layer (probabilistic mitigations, cheap first filter): an injection/jailbreak detection classifier (Llama Guard / Prompt Guard-style or a fine-tuned classifier) on untrusted inputs; spotlighting/datamarking — wrap retrieved notes/reviews and user text in delimiters and label them as data, never instructions; sanitize retrieved content (strip zero-width/hidden characters, suspicious markup) at ingestion, not just query time. All of these are detection, not prevention. Model/orchestration layer: least-privilege capability scoping — the authenticated user id comes from the session, never from anything the model emits, so the model cannot choose whose orders to act on; keep trusted policy separate from untrusted data; use constrained tool-calling with argument-schema validation. Tool/output layer (deterministic enforcement — the real trust boundary): authorization checks inside each tool (issue_refund and lookup_order verify the order belongs to the session user; the $500 cap stays in code); send_email restricted by allowlist to the authenticated user's own verified address; a policy engine that validates every proposed tool call (amount, ownership, recipient) before execution; human-in-the-loop / step-up auth for irreversible or high-risk actions; output scanning for other-customer PII before send.

(c) In finding (1) the user is the attacker and the payload is in their own turn; 'I'm a manager' is a privilege claim the model cannot grant — roles come from auth, not assertions — and the cap + ownership + recipient allowlist make 'refund tenfold' and 'email attacker@evil.com' impossible regardless of compliance. Finding (2) is indirect injection: a third party planted content that enters via RAG, the victim is a different user, the user may be benign, and it evades any classifier watching the user turn and can fire silently. Defenses: treat ALL retrieved content as untrusted, scan/strip at ingestion, and rely on tool-layer authorization so a successful injection still cannot email another customer's data externally. Best of all, design the arbitrary-recipient capability out.

(d) Testing: build a threat model and attack taxonomy (direct jailbreaks, indirect injection per untrusted field, privilege-escalation claims, exfiltration, cap-bypass, argument tampering); red-team with curated known attacks plus automated/generated payloads, seeding malicious content into order notes/reviews to cover the indirect channel; freeze every successful attack into a CI regression suite that runs on every model or prompt change (both drift). Primary metric: Attack Success Rate per category, driven down and reported with confidence intervals — never claim 0%. Balance it against benign over-refusal/false-positive rate and added latency. The point of defense-in-depth is that one layer's residual bypass is not catastrophic.
